# Designing with SystemVerilog {#sec-sv-design .unnumbered}

## Goal for this week

- Describe combinational logic with `always_comb`, and sequential logic with
  `always_ff`, using the assignment operator each one requires
- Recognize latch inference on sight, and write code that cannot produce one
- Choose between synchronous and asynchronous reset
- Build a design from smaller ones with module instances and parameters
- Write a testbench that drives a design and checks its outputs

## Two kinds of logic, two kinds of block

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| | Combinational | Sequential |
|---|---|---|
| Output depends on | current inputs | inputs **and** stored state |
| Block | `always_comb` | `always_ff @(posedge clk)` |
| Assignment | blocking `=` | non-blocking `<=` |
| Hardware | gates, multiplexers | flip-flops |

- `assign` is the one-line form of combinational logic
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The previous chapter described combinational logic one line at a time with
`assign`. That works for an adder or a small multiplexer, but it gets
awkward the moment a function needs an `if` or a `case`. For those we use
**procedural blocks**: a block of statements that describes how a set of
outputs depends on a set of inputs.

SystemVerilog has two procedural blocks for synthesizable hardware, and
which one you pick is not a matter of taste. It is dictated by what you are
building:

| | Combinational | Sequential |
|---|---|---|
| Output depends on | current inputs only | inputs **and** stored state |
| Block | `always_comb` | `always_ff @(posedge clk)` |
| Assignment | blocking, `=` | non-blocking, `<=` |
| Hardware | gates, multiplexers | flip-flops |

The `_comb` and `_ff` in the names are a promise to the tool: if the code
inside does not describe the kind of hardware its block name claims, the
tool reports it. Older Verilog has a single `always @(...)` for both
purposes, and a whole class of bugs came from getting it wrong without any
warning.
:::

## Combinational logic: `always_comb`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module inverter (
    input  logic a,
    output logic y
);
  always_comb begin
    y = ~a;
  end
endmodule
```

- Re-evaluates whenever **any signal it reads** changes
- Statements run in order: use blocking `=`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
An `always_comb` block re-evaluates itself whenever any signal it reads
changes. It is closer to a spreadsheet formula that recalculates on every
input edit than to a function you call:

```systemverilog
module inverter (
    input  logic a,
    output logic y
);
  always_comb begin
    y = ~a;
  end
endmodule
```

You do not write a sensitivity list: the tool works it out from the
signals the block reads. Assignment inside it uses `=`, the **blocking**
assignment, which reads as "this is what the output equals right now". Inside
one block, blocking assignments take effect in the order they are written,
so a later statement sees the result of an earlier one.
:::

## `if` and `case`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module mux4to1_case (
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    input  logic [3:0] d,
    output logic       y
);
  always_comb begin
    case (sel)
      2'b00:   y = d[0];
      2'b01:   y = d[1];
      2'b10:   y = d[2];
      2'b11:   y = d[3];
      default: y = 1'b0;
    endcase
  end
endmodule
```

- Always write a `default`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A multiplexer with more than two inputs is clearer as a `case` statement
than as a chain of `?:` operators:

```systemverilog
module mux4to1_case (
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    input  logic [3:0] d,
    output logic       y
);
  always_comb begin
    case (sel)
      2'b00:   y = d[0];
      2'b01:   y = d[1];
      2'b10:   y = d[2];
      2'b11:   y = d[3];
      default: y = 1'b0;     // also covers sel containing X or Z
    endcase
  end
endmodule
```

The `case` compares `sel` against each listed value in turn and runs the
matching branch. It describes the same multiplexer as the nested
conditional operator in the previous chapter, only in a form that scales to
eight or sixteen inputs without becoming unreadable. The `default` branch is
the safety net, and the next section explains why it is not optional.
:::

## The latch trap

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (input_button) begin
    status = 1'b1;
    result = 1'b0;
  end else if (done_signal) begin
    status = 1'b0;
  end
end
```

**Discussion question:** what is `result` when `done_signal` is high? And
what are `status` and `result` when both inputs are low?
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Here is a block that looks complete and is not:

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (input_button) begin
    status = 1'b1;
    result = 1'b0;
  end else if (done_signal) begin
    status = 1'b0;
  end
end
```

Ask what `result` equals when `done_signal` is high: no branch says. And
what are `status` and `result` when both inputs are low? Again, no branch
says. In a spreadsheet, an unhandled case would show a blank cell. In
hardware, an output cannot go blank. If no branch assigns it, the only way
to keep it at *some* value is to remember the previous one, so the
synthesizer builds a **latch**: a level-sensitive memory element
(@fig-latch). That is almost never what you want in a synchronous design.
It adds a storage element you did not intend, it breaks timing analysis,
and it is the most common bug `always_comb` produces.

![What synthesis builds for an incomplete `if`: a latch whose enable is `sel`, so the output holds its old value whenever `sel` is 0.](../images/rtl/latch_bug.svg){#fig-latch width=70%}

The rule is that every signal assigned in an `always_comb` block must be
assigned on **every** path through it. The most reliable way to follow it is
to give every output a default value at the top of the block, and let the
branches override it:

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  status = 1'b0;               // defaults: every path assigns both outputs
  result = 1'b0;
  if (input_button)
    status = 1'b1;
  else if (done_signal)
    status = 1'b0;
end
```

With the defaults in place, a forgotten `else` is harmless. If you really
do want a latch, SystemVerilog has a block for it, `always_latch`, which
documents the intent. Tools also warn when `always_comb` would infer one,
which is the reason to use it instead of the old `always @(*)`.
:::

## Sequential logic: `always_ff`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module dff (
    input  logic clk, d,
    output logic q
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    q <= d;
  end
endmodule
```

- Runs **only** on the clock edge named in `@(...)`
- Non-blocking `<=`: "schedule this update at the edge"
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
`always_ff` describes a block that updates only at a clock edge: a
register, not a formula. The sensitivity list is not optional here. It names
the event that triggers the block:

```systemverilog
module dff (
    input  logic clk, d,
    output logic q
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    q <= d;
  end
endmodule
```

On every rising edge of `clk` the block runs and copies `d` into `q`. At any
other moment nothing happens, and `q` holds its value: that holding is the
memory. The operator is `<=`, the **non-blocking** assignment. It reads as
"at this clock edge, schedule this update", rather than `=`'s "this is the
value right now". `always_ff` tells the tool that this block must infer
flip-flops, and it reports a warning if the code would produce anything
else.
:::

## Blocking vs. non-blocking

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  a <= b;
  b <= a;     // swap: works
end
```

| | `=` blocking | `<=` non-blocking |
|---|---|---|
| Statements | one after another | all at once |
| Use in | `always_comb` | `always_ff` |

- No exceptions to this pairing
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The difference between the two operators matters the moment two registers
depend on each other, which is exactly the situation of every pipeline
register. Consider two registers meant to swap values on the same clock
edge:

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  a <= b;
  b <= a;
end
```

With non-blocking assignment, both right-hand sides are read using each
register's value *before* this clock edge, and both updates take effect
together. The swap works, which matches what "on every clock edge, in
parallel" should mean. Replace `<=` with `=` and the second line reads the
value the first line just wrote, collapsing two parallel updates into a
sequential one: both registers end up holding `b`, and nothing about the
syntax warns you.

| | Blocking `=` | Non-blocking `<=` |
|---|---|---|
| Statements in a block | take effect one after another | all take effect together |
| Reads the value of | the latest assignment | the value before the clock edge |
| Use in | `always_comb` | `always_ff` |

That is why the pairing has no exceptions: `=` in combinational logic, `<=`
in clocked logic, every time. A group of non-blocking statements is
evaluated concurrently, in the same sense that the `assign` statements in
the previous chapter are.

Putting both block types together gives the smallest useful piece of a
pipeline stage: a multiplexer feeding a register. The `always_comb` block
becomes the mux, the `always_ff` block becomes the flip-flop, and the only
wire between them is `y` (@fig-mux2-reg).

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = in1;
  else     y = in0;
end

always_ff @(posedge clk) q <= y;
```

![Synthesized result of the code above, drawn by Yosys from the full module in `images/rtl/mux2_reg.sv`: the mux feeds the D input of an 8-bit register.](../images/rtl/mux2_reg.svg){#fig-mux2-reg width=80%}
:::

## Reset styles

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
// Synchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```

```systemverilog
// Asynchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A register that starts in an unknown state is a bug waiting to happen, so
registers get a reset. There are two ways to write it, and both clear `q` to
zero when `reset` is high. They differ in *when* the clear can happen.

```systemverilog
// Synchronous reset: only looked at on a clock edge
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end

// Asynchronous reset: acts the moment reset asserts
always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```

A **synchronous** reset takes effect only at a clock edge. `reset` is just
another input to the logic that decides the next value of `q`. In a generic
design that is a little logic in front of the D input, although the
flip-flops of an FPGA slice have a dedicated set/reset input that absorbs it
(@fig-counter shows the flip-flop with its reset input). An **asynchronous** reset takes effect the
moment `reset` asserts, regardless of the clock, which is why it appears in
the sensitivity list next to `posedge clk`. It needs a flip-flop with a
dedicated reset pin, and the moment it is released matters: if `reset`
deasserts too close to a clock edge, the flip-flop can misbehave. We come
back to that when we discuss synchronizers.

For now, the practical rule: pick one style, use it everywhere in a design,
and know which one you picked.
:::

## Example: a counter

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module counter4 (
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       reset,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
    else       count <= count + 1;
  end
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A 4-bit counter that counts on the rising clock edge, with a synchronous
active-high reset, is a register whose next value is its own current value
plus one:

```systemverilog
module counter4 (
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       reset,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
    else       count <= count + 1;
  end
endmodule
```

On every rising edge, if `reset` is high the counter returns to zero.
Otherwise it increments. When it reaches `4'b1111`, the next `+ 1` wraps
around to `4'b0000` because the result is truncated to 4 bits. The tool
builds exactly what the text says (@fig-counter): a 4-bit adder, a flip-flop
with a synchronous reset, and the feedback wire from the register back to
the adder. The output `count` is the register itself, so it needs no extra
`assign`.

![The `counter4` module, drawn by Yosys: the register output feeds both the output port and the adder, and `reset` drives the synchronous reset input.](../images/rtl/counter4.svg){#fig-counter}

@fig-counter-wave shows its behavior over time. The output is unknown until
the first clock edge samples `reset` high, then it counts up by one on every
edge.

![Timing of `counter4`: `count` changes only just after a rising clock edge.](../images/waves/counter.svg){#fig-counter-wave}
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
1. `assign` inside a procedural block
2. Several blocks driving the same signal
3. An unassigned path in `always_comb`: a latch

Every one of them compiles in some tools and breaks in others.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Three mistakes account for most of the broken designs in a first course.

**1. An `assign` inside a block.** `assign` is a module-level statement. It
does not belong inside `always_comb`, where plain `=` is used:

```systemverilog
// Wrong
always_comb begin
  assign c = a & b;
end

// Right
always_comb begin
  c = a & b;
end
```

**2. More than one driver for a signal.** Every signal must be written by
exactly one `always_ff`, one `always_comb`, or one `assign`, never a mix:

```systemverilog
// Wrong: c has three drivers
always_ff @(posedge clk) c <= {x, 1'b0};
always_comb              c = x;
assign                   c = in1 + in2;
```

Hardware cannot have three sources driving one wire. The tools reject this
for `logic`, and for a `wire` it would produce an `X` like the two-driver
example in the previous chapter.

**3. A path that does not assign an output.** This is the latch trap from
earlier in the chapter: every output assigned on every path, and defaults
at the top of the block to make sure of it.
:::

## Structural modeling: module instances

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module mux2to1 (
    input  logic a, b, sel,
    output logic y
);
  assign y = sel ? b : a;
endmodule
```

```systemverilog
mux2to1 mux_low (
    .a(d[0]), .b(d[1]), .sel(sel[0]), .y(y0)
);
```

- *module name*, *instance name*, *port connections*
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
So far we described a module by what it *does*, which is called behavioral
modeling. **Structural modeling** describes a module by how it is *composed*
of simpler modules. Each copy of a smaller module is an **instance**, and it
has a unique name.

Here a 4:1 multiplexer is assembled from three copies of a 2:1 multiplexer:

```systemverilog
module mux2to1 (
    input  logic a, b, sel,
    output logic y
);
  assign y = sel ? b : a;
endmodule

module mux4to1_struct (
    input  logic [3:0] d,
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    output logic       y
);
  logic y0, y1;                 // wires between the instances

  mux2to1 mux_low   (.a(d[0]), .b(d[1]), .sel(sel[0]), .y(y0));
  mux2to1 mux_high  (.a(d[2]), .b(d[3]), .sel(sel[0]), .y(y1));
  mux2to1 mux_final (.a(y0),   .b(y1),   .sel(sel[1]), .y(y));
endmodule
```

An instantiation has three parts. First comes the **module name**
(`mux2to1`), then the **instance name** you choose (`mux_final`), then in
parentheses the **port connections**. The notation `.a(y0)` reads "the
module's port `a` is connected to my signal `y0`". These connections by
name make the code easy to read and safe to reorder. There is also a
positional form, `mux2to1 mux_final (y0, y1, sel[1], y);`, which is shorter
and fails silently if someone later reorders the ports, so we avoid it.

@fig-mux4-struct shows the result. Unlike the earlier schematics, the tool
leaves the three instances as boxes instead of expanding them into gates,
which is exactly how the hierarchy appears in your code.

![The structurally built `mux4to1_struct`: two instances select within a pair, and a third selects between the two results.](../images/rtl/mux4to1_struct.svg){#fig-mux4-struct width=80%}
:::

## Parameters

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module counter #(
    parameter WIDTH = 8
) (
    input  logic             clk, reset,
    output logic [WIDTH-1:0] count
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= '0;
    else       count <= count + 1;
  end
endmodule
```

```systemverilog
counter #(.WIDTH(16)) counter_inst (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
All the modules so far had fixed widths. A **parameter** makes a module
configurable: the same description works for any width, and each instance
picks its own.

```systemverilog
module counter #(
    parameter WIDTH = 8              // default if an instance omits it
) (
    input  logic             clk,
    input  logic             reset,
    output logic [WIDTH-1:0] count
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= '0;
    else       count <= count + 1;
  end
endmodule
```

The parameter list sits between the module name and the port list, after a
`#`. An instance overrides it the same way, by name:

```systemverilog
module top (
    input  logic        clk,
    input  logic        reset,
    output logic [15:0] count
);
  counter #(.WIDTH(16)) counter_inst (
      .clk(clk),
      .reset(reset),
      .count(count)
  );
endmodule
```

The literal `'0` in the reset branch means "all zeros, whatever the width",
which is what lets one description serve every `WIDTH`. A `localparam` is
a constant inside a module that, unlike a `parameter`, cannot be
overridden from outside, which makes it the right tool for derived constants:

```systemverilog
localparam CNT_WIDTH = 16;
counter #(.WIDTH(CNT_WIDTH)) counter_inst (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));
```
:::

## Testbenches

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module tb_mux4to1;
  logic [3:0] d;
  logic [1:0] sel;
  logic       y;

  mux4to1_struct dut (.d(d), .sel(sel), .y(y));

  initial begin
    d = 4'b1010;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) begin
      sel = i[1:0];
      #10;
      if (y !== d[sel]) $error("sel=%b: y=%b", sel, y);
    end
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A **testbench** is a module that tests another module, the *device under
test* (DUT). It applies inputs to the DUT and, ideally, checks that the
outputs are right. Its inputs and the expected outputs are the *test
vectors*. A testbench has no ports of its own: it sits at the top of the
simulation, so everything it needs is declared inside as plain `logic`
signals and wired to the DUT by name, like any other instance.

```systemverilog
module tb_mux4to1;
  logic [3:0] d;
  logic [1:0] sel;
  logic       y;

  mux4to1_struct dut (.d(d), .sel(sel), .y(y));

  initial begin
    d = 4'b1010;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) begin
      sel = i[1:0];
      #10;
      $display("d=%b sel=%b y=%b", d, sel, y);
      if (y !== d[sel]) $error("sel=%b: expected %b, got %b", sel, d[sel], y);
    end
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

Everything happens in the `initial` block, which starts at time zero and
runs once. It holds `d` fixed and sweeps `sel` through all four values. After
each change it waits `#10` time units, `$display` prints the inputs and the
output, and the `if` checks `y` against the bit of `d` that `sel` selects.
The `#10` delay is not needed by the circuit, since a combinational output
settles almost instantly. It gives each test case its own slice of
simulation time, so the printed lines and the waveform stay readable. The
comparison uses `!==`, which also catches an `X` on the output where `!=`
would stay silent. `$finish` ends the simulation.

These statements (`initial`, `#10`, `$display`, `$finish`) exist only in
simulation. A synthesizer has no hardware for "wait 10 time units", which is
the line between the code you simulate and the code you synthesize.
:::

## Testbench for a sequential design

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module tb_counter;
  logic       clk = 0;
  logic       reset = 1;
  logic [3:0] count;

  counter #(.WIDTH(4)) dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));

  always #5 clk = ~clk;              // clock generator

  initial begin
    #12 reset = 0;
    #100;
    $display("count=%0d", count);
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

- The testbench must **supply the clock**
- `$finish` is essential: the clock never stops
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A registered design only changes on a clock edge, so the testbench has to
supply that clock; nothing else in the simulation will.

```systemverilog
module tb_counter;
  logic       clk = 0;
  logic       reset = 1;
  logic [3:0] count;

  counter #(.WIDTH(4)) dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));

  always #5 clk = ~clk;              // clock generator: period of 10 units

  initial begin
    #12 reset = 0;                   // release reset between clock edges
    #100;
    $display("count=%0d", count);
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

The separate `always #5 clk = ~clk;` has no sensitivity list and no guard,
so it keeps re-executing for the whole simulation and flips `clk` every 5
time units. That gives a free-running clock with a period of 10. It runs
concurrently with the `initial` block below it: every `initial` and
`always` block in a module starts at time zero and proceeds independently,
which is why the clock generator lives in its own block.

The stimulus holds `reset` high for the first clock edge (at time 5), then
releases it at time 12, between edges, so that no input changes exactly
when the clock rises. After the remaining ten rising edges the counter holds
10, which `$display` prints. The key difference from the combinational
testbench is the waiting. A combinational output is valid almost
immediately after its inputs change, but a register updates only once per
clock edge, so a sequential testbench must always budget enough simulated
time, or wait for a specific number of `@(posedge clk)` events, before
checking the outputs.

`$finish` matters even more here. The clock generator never terminates on
its own, so without an explicit `$finish` the simulation would run forever.
:::

## Running a simulation

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```bash
iverilog -g2012 -o sim_counter counter.sv tb_counter.sv
vvp sim_counter
```

- Add `$dumpfile` / `$dumpvars` to write a waveform for GTKWave
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Any SystemVerilog simulator can run these testbenches. With the open-source
Icarus Verilog, you compile the design together with its testbench and run
the result:

```bash
iverilog -g2012 -o sim_counter counter.sv tb_counter.sv
vvp sim_counter
```

The `-g2012` option selects the SystemVerilog language level. To look at
waveforms instead of printed lines, add two statements at the start of the
`initial` block, and open the resulting file in GTKWave:

```systemverilog
$dumpfile("tb_counter.vcd");
$dumpvars(0, tb_counter);
```

Checking results by eye in a waveform does not scale beyond a handful of
signals. A testbench that compares outputs against expected values, as ours
does with `$error`, can be run again after every change and report a clear
pass or fail. Later in the course we move this idea to a Python framework,
cocotb, which makes writing such checks much easier.
:::

## From design to the pipeline

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `always_comb` and `always_ff`: the two blocks every design is built from
- Instances and parameters: how small blocks become a system
- Next: these constructs, applied to a real five-stage pipeline
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Everything introduced here is the working vocabulary of the rest of the
course. `always_ff` with non-blocking assignment and a reset is how every
pipeline register is built. `always_comb` with defaults at the top is how
the ALU and the decoder avoid latch inference. Module instances and
parameters are how those pieces are assembled into stages and stages into
a processor. The pipeline chapters introduce no new syntax: they put these
constructs to work on a larger example.
:::
